Jamadagni
------------------------------------------
Listed among the Saptarṣis—the group of seven great sages—and the gotrapravartakas (originators of lineages), जमदग्नि was the son of the sage ऋचीक and the princess सत्यवती. He had married रेणुका, the daughter of a king, Prasenajit.
He had five sons, of whom the famous Paraśurāma—considered as a partial इन्चर्नतिओन् of Viṣṇu—was the last.
Once, जमदग्नि suspected the fidelity of his wife रेणुका and ordered his sons to behead her. The first four refused and were cursed by him. But, परशुराम complied with the command. Pleased at his obedience, जमदग्नि granted him a boon. Then परशुराम asked for the revival of his मोथेर्, withdrawal of the curse against his elder brothers and also requested that he give up his irascible temperament. जमदग्नि agreed for all.
Jamadagni was killed by शूरसेन, the son of Kārtavīrya-अर्जुन, since he had refused to hand over the celestial cow Kapilā. This was the main reason for परशुराम’s tours of conquest against the kṣattriyas to destroy them.
See also PARAŚURĀMA.

Jāmbavān
------------------------------------------
The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि which describes the story of राम, has many interesting personalities involved in the story. One such—the wise old man—is जाम्बवान्. He is said to have sprung out of the mouth of ब्रह्मा, the creator, when he once yawned (jṛbhaṇa = yawning). He was the king of bhallūkas or bears. He had an unusually long span of life and had witnessed many a battle between the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस् (demons). He had helped the gods during the churning of the ocean (samudramathana), had drunk the अमृत (ambrosia or nectar) and had become very strong.
During a sacrifice performed by the asura king बलि, he was in charge of medicinal herbs.
He was a great devotee of शिव and used to visit कैलास regularly every day.
He was at first the commander-in-chief of वालि and later on switched over his loyalties to सुग्रीव after the latter’s banishment. He was one of the prominent members of the group of monkeys that was sent to the south by सुग्रीव, in search of सीता. It was he who encouraged and inspired the monkeys when they were very much dejected by not finding सीता. Again, it was he who inspired हनुमान् to cross the ocean to bring the news of सीता.
During the रामायण war, he rendered invaluable help, especially by his sage counsels and timely intervention.
When कृष्ण was implicated in the loss of the Syamantakamaṇi—a jewel that used to give a lot of gold every day—he traced the jewel ultimately to जाम्बवान्’s cave. कृष्ण fought with him for 28 days before vanquishing him. जाम्बवान् had to concede defeat and give, not only the jewel, but also his daughter Jāmbavatī, in मर्रिअगे.
See also SYAMANTAKAMAṆI.
